/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.headline: Friday briefing: How a leaderless student group is challenging power in Serbia
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.excerpt: Good morning. As waves of youth-led protests swell across Europe, prompted by the cost of living, unaffordable housing and education standards, in Serbia the younger generation is taking on the apparatus of the state itself. In tight-run parliamentary elections this Sunday, the country’s most consequential political movement in decades, Student List, is challenging former Slobodan Milošević henchman Aleksandar Vučić and his 12-year domination of Serbian politics. Two years on from a singular national tragedy that galvanised public anger at state cover-ups and corruption, gen Z have channelled their energy and fury into a bold experiment in direct democracy, creating a genuinely leaderless, grassroots movement that is firing up disaffected voters across the country. I spoke to Julian Borger, our senior international correspondent, who has just returned from Belgrade, about their hopes of emulating the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary and the potential for a democratic domino through central Europe. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.trail: In today’s newsletter: ​Born from the fury surrounding the deadly Novi Sad station collapse, Serbia’s Student List has taken its protests all the way to the elections in an unprecedented grassroots campaign

/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.headline: Serbian prosecutor who investigated Belgrade Trump tower project ‘targeted with spyware’
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.excerpt: A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help the Trumps build a tower in Belgrade has been targeted with advanced spyware, expert analysis indicates. The finding suggests a disturbing new element in the authoritarian Serbian regime’s campaign to undermine what is believed to be the first criminal case related to global moneymaking drive of the US president’s family, which critics describe as a “pay to play” scheme trading the Trump administration’s favour for business opportunities. Rade Bajić, the targeted prosecutor, said: “In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack.” Analysts at the Citizen Lab, a digital forensics laboratory, have not so far established who was behind the attack but the Serbian regime has previously been caught using spyware against its opponents. News of the alleged hack follows the Guardian’s revelations last week that Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s president, personally ordered that a cherished site in Belgrade be stripped of its legal protection so it could be handed over for a $500m Trump hotel and tower. Vučić, one of the Balkans’ most influential nationalists, hosted the US president’s son Donald Jr – “dear Don”, as he calls him – and son-in-law Jared Kushner as he ingratiated himself with the Trumps. At the weekend, Vučić responded to the Guardian’s revelations about his role in the scandal by confirming details of a previously secret meeting.

/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.headline: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.excerpt: Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal. Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office. The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates. The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption. A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios. After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.

/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.headline: Kosovo’s former president jailed for 25 years over war crimes
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.excerpt: Hashim Thaçi, the former president of Kosovo, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a tribunal in The Hague for war crimes, including dozens of murders, committed during his time as a senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army during the country’s war for independence from Serbia in the late 1990s. The European-backed Kosovo Specialist Chambers, convicted Thaci, 58, and three other former senior commanders of 96 murders, and counts of torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention directed at political opponents and civilians. The convictions come at the end of a years-long process, strongly opposed by many in Kosovo, to bring accountability for crimes committed by KLA commanders during the 1998-99 war in which war crimes were committed by both sides. Thaçi, who resigned from office nearly six years ago to face charges, stood in silence in The Hague as the presiding judge Charles Smith read out the sentence. The former president, who served as the head of political directorate of the KLA’s general staff, faced multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity alongside the three other former leaders of the KLA who are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland. In addition to the murders, Thaçi was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of about 50.
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.trail: Hashim Thaçi, 58, was convicted by The Hague for crimes committed while he was senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army

/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.headline: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, given hero’s funeral in Serbia
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.excerpt: Ratko Mladić, a Serbian general convicted of orchestrating the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war, has been given a hero’s funeral attended by thousands in Belgrade despite international alarm. Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia” for his role during the Balkans genocide in the 1990s, Mladić died in prison in late August aged 84 while serving a life sentence for war crimes and crimes against humanity. Mladić was found guilty of genocide in 2017 for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the UN-designated enclave. But he has remained a beloved figure among many Serbs, with the president, Aleksandar Vučić, arguing last month for him to be released early from a UN detention facility in The Hague so he could die on Serbian soil. Vučić, an ultranationalist leader, has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade and is due to run again for prime minister in a snap election announced on Monday. Mladić’s coffin was flown to Serbia last week on a government plane, draped in national flags and carried from the aircraft by uniformed soldiers. On Monday morning, thousands of people gathered in front of a small church in the Serbian capital to pay their respects to Mladić. Armed forces stood guard at his casket, on top of which was laid his signature military cap, as well as a sword. A display of medals lay in front.
/world/2026/oct/25/serbian-leader-aleksa.trail: Fanfare at Belgrade funeral of man convicted of genocide raises questions from EU over Serbia’s membership plan

/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.headline: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.excerpt: Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc. The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU. Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU. In an interview with the Sunday Times, he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.” Burnham has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union. It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029. Burnham acknowledged freedom of movement had “very significant challenges associated with it”, but he suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade. “It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times. “Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then?
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.trail: Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November

/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.headline: Can curry nights and canny advisers help Healey deliver a budget for everyday people?
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.excerpt: Every Sunday night, the chancellor, John Healey, slips next door to Andy Burnham’s Downing Street flat where they order a curry and chew over politics on the prime minister’s sofa. An Indian takeaway is one of the totemic issues in British politics, a “treat” fewer people can afford, like a pint at the football or soft play for the kids. Healey has promised to give Britain’s battered consumers “breathing space” in next week’s budget, but three months after taking on the job, the new chancellor also hopes to buy himself time. Key decisions will be postponed until a spending review at some point next year – including when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence: the issue that prompted Healey’s resignation as defence secretary in June, hastening Keir Starmer’s departure. The weekly curry summit is a chance, as some aides see it, to separate Healey from cautious Treasury officials, and get him to kick around the politics. With just a few days to go before the budget, every adviser and official remarks on how closely the prime minister is involved: not just in decision-making, but in the process and politics – unlike Starmer. “Keir wanted to be presented with three ideas and then pick one,” one aide says. “But, actually, in politics, sometimes you need to bash things around and come up with ideas.
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.trail: The chancellor has promised ‘breathing space’ for households and small businesses but global events cannot be ignored

/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.headline: Potholes, bus fares and headphone dodgers: will Burnham’s strategy of ‘everyday fixes’ succeed?
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.excerpt: In the first episode of Armando Iannucci’s political satire The Thick of It, the hapless minister Hugh Abbot is in the back of a taxi, frantically brainstorming for an on-the-hoof policy he can announce to the assembled national press. “So you want something sexy and eye-catching, and that is free and universally popular and instantly applicable. No one can possibly object to it,” says the addled junior adviser Ollie Reeder. “Well, really, you should have said something before then, because I’ve got a file about that fucking thick of that back in the office.” After a three-month micro-policy blitz from Downing Street, the question now being asked is: did Reeder pass said file on to the government’s battalion of special advisers? In the past week Andy Burnham has vowed to clamp down on social pariahs blaring out TikTok videos on public transport, outlaw “rip-off” private car park fines and – on Thursday – fill in potholes in 7,000 miles of England’s roads. Before that, as part of the focus on “everyday fixes”, the prime minister announced a plan to remove VAT from electricity bills, a £2 cap on single bus fares across England and take action on “auto-renew” subscriptions. There’s also promises to crack down on pricey branded school uniforms, ban specious discounts, limit vape and betting shops and stop airlines charging families to sit together on planes. At this rate all minor annoyances in the UK will be eradicated by Christmas. The idea is simple, says one policy adviser.
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.trail: New PM has prioritised small fixes to show voters Labour can make a real difference, and government insiders are delighted at the public’s reaction

/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.headline: Tax online sales more heavily to save high streets, Burnham urged
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.excerpt: Andy Burnham has been urged by one of his most senior former advisers to tax internet sales more heavily than in-store purchases to help “level the playing field” for struggling high streets. As the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, prepare for their first budget next week, Andy Haldane joined calls for action to stop more shops closing across the UK. In an interview for a Guardian series looking at how Britain can reverse the declining fortunes of towns, the former Bank of England chief economist urged them to launch a realignment of the tax system away from favouring online sellers, alongside a review of business rates and measures to turbocharge devolution. “The balance of tax incentives are strongly skewed towards the digital over the physical, and the large over small, and if you’re serious about high streets that needs somehow rebalancing,” he said. Calling on Burnham to follow through with Labour’s manifesto promise to “replace” the business rates system, Haldane said “some levelling of the playing field” was needed to help smaller operators who faced soaring costs and evaporating demand. “One of the reasons why high streets are dying, and some of the towns, is business rates are punitive for smaller shops,” he said. “This needs to be wrapped up with that more fundamental review of business rates and I’ll hope we see that in the budget.
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.trail: Exclusive: British Chambers of Commerce president calls for overhaul of business rates and greater powers for local leaders

/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.headline: Wanted: new No 10 adviser to help citizens deal with rise of AI
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.excerpt: Andy Burnham is to recruit a number of advisers to plug gaps in No 10, including an expert on how AI will affect society. The roles advertised by Downing Street give a glimpse into the biggest challenges facing the prime minister – and what he has decided to prioritise. The new hires will flesh out the threadbare No 10 policy unit – where many of the roles are still vacant after Keir Starmer’s departure. Senior sources have said the prime minister wanted to take time to recruit advisers. The adviser on AI, who will be expected to have “deep expertise” in the sector, will be expected to lead preparations for the impact of the AI boom on the workforce, amid significant concerns for lower-level professional services jobs, in particular for new graduates. They will also be expected to be the main adviser to Burnham on frontier AI, the effects and benefits of AI in public service transformation and other major societal impacts. Several cabinet ministers have openly expressed concerns about the UK’s readiness for the impact of AI on the workforce and economy, as well as the dangers of unregulated systems. In his Labour conference speech on 28 September, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said there were “daunting” dangers of AI, saying they could not allow technological advances “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.
/politics/2026/oct/25/burnham-rayner-lab.trail: Andy Burnham advertises for policy experts in technology, economic growth and cost-of-living challenges

/uk-news/2026/oct/25/storm-boelo-warning.headline: Summer of 2026 was UK’s hottest on record, Met Office says
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/storm-boelo-warning.excerpt: This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data, and the Met Office said the season’s mean temperature was made 130 times more likely by the climate crisis. Record-breaking and back-to-back heatwaves have scorched much of Europe. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’s hottest since records began in 1884. Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels. The Met Office said an average mean UK temperature of 16.5C made this summer provisionally the warmest on record as well as the warmest season in a series going back to 1884. England, Wales and Northern Ireland broke their respective mean temperature records for summer while Scotland recorded its joint sixth hottest summer. This is the second year in a row that temperature records have been broken, with 2025 and 2026 both the warmest UK summers since records began. The infamous summer of 1976 is now the seventh warmest on record in terms of mean temperature. Katie White, the minister for climate transition, said it was a “brutal reminder that we’re not waiting for climate change to arrive in Britain, we’re living in the middle of it.
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/storm-boelo-warning.trail: Meteorologists say mean average temperature of 16.5C was made 130 times more likely by climate crisis

/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.headline: What has Burnham promised since he became PM, and when will it happen?
/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.excerpt: Andy Burnham has floated a number of policies, ideas and ambitions for his government since becoming prime minister, from shifting power out of Westminster, bringing services under public control and addressing the rising cost of living. But many of his promises are not actually firm commitments, so what has he pledged, how much will it cost and when should the public expect change? Cutting VAT from household electricity bills On his second day as prime minister, Burnham promised to scrap VAT on household electricity bills from October. He announced the immediate tax cut to help ease cost-of-living pressures. The government said the move would reduce the average household’s electricity bill by £45, though the actual saving could depend on how much each household used. Burnham said it would be funded by ending Keir Starmer’s digital ID scheme, which would have cost the government £1.8bn over three years. Darren Jones, the former chief secretary to Starmer when he was PM, claimed the money for the digital ID scheme was still unfunded, however, and said Burnham would have to set out how he would pay for his new policies at the budget. £2 bus fares Single bus fares across England will be capped at £2 from January, down £1 from the current maximum, which reverses the increase Starmer and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves put in place in 2024. The cap will last until the end of 2027 and excludes London.
/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.trail: From cutting household bills to moving power out of Westminster, how will the measures announced unfold?

/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.headline: Rough sleepers wary of Burnham pledge: ‘So you mean he has said some words?’
/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.excerpt: As Andy Burnham set out his plan to end rough sleeping on Tuesday night, volunteers from homelessness charity Under One Sky were offering hot drinks, sandwiches, socks, underwear and soap to dozens of rough sleepers around Tottenham Court Road in central London. Among those sleeping on the streets, the prime minister’s plan was met with widespread scepticism born from long familiarity with similar political declarations. “You can never end rough sleeping. I think he is taking on a monumental task,” said a former construction worker in his 50s, who did not want to be named. He was living in a hostel after struggling to find work over the past few years, and was reluctant to sign on for unemployment benefits. “[Burnham] has committed himself to the target; if he doesn’t fulfil it, there will be problems. I wouldn’t have done that,” he said. Many said it was hard to follow the news without regular internet access, but several were aware that Burnham had made a commitment to end rough sleeping when he came to power. “He has made a pledge? You mean he has said some words?” said one man in his 60s who has been sleeping intermittently in a tent in front of a furniture shop for several years. He was reluctant to say why he was homeless, only that he had previously owned a restaurant before losing his house. He chose to stay in his spot on the street because of the easy access to a nearby hospital, and said he was not looking for any help from the government.
/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.trail: On drive to end rough sleeping, homeless people and charities say they have heard similar declarations before

/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.headline: Burnham launches ‘national drive’ to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.excerpt: Andy Burnham has urged local leaders to offer all rough sleepers in England a route off the streets by Christmas, as he pledges another £100m to end street homelessness. Arguing in the Guardian that rough sleeping has become so common it now “feels like part of the scenery”, Burnham promised he would mount a Covid-style campaign to get everyone off the streets this winter. The announcement solidifies tackling homelessness as a central policy for Burnham’s government, and gives voters a measure by which to judge his success – although without a concrete target for ministers to hit. Homelessness campaigners welcomed the move, but warned more will need to be done to tackle the longer-term temporary accommodation crisis, which has given the UK the worst homelessness problem in the western world. In his article for the Guardian, the prime minister writes: “We see people bedded down in doorways and sat outside stations, carrying their lives in rucksacks and sleeping bags on their backs. And I think most people have the same reaction: this isn’t right. “It shouldn’t be happening here. But we’ve lived with it for so long that something that used to shock us now feels like part of the scenery.” He adds: “We did it in the pandemic. We got people out of the cold because, as a country, we decided it had to be done. We can do it again. “That’s why the first thing I announced when I became prime minister was a commitment to end rough sleeping.
/society/2026/oct/25/homelessness-rough-.trail: Prime minister urges local leaders to act as homelessness campaigners welcome move but say more needs to be done

/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.headline: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.excerpt: Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president. The prosecutor’s office in the southern city of Nice said on Sunday that 59 people had been taken into police custody, including 11 suspected of belonging to extreme-right groups. They were alleged to have gathered with the intent of committing violence. Some were arrested in two vehicles with masks, gloves, gas sprays and truncheons, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement to public broadcaster FranceInfo. Local media in Nice had reported extreme-right groups coming to the city centre and targeting demonstrators on Saturday. In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions. The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.trail: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres

/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.headline: France to deploy 70,000 police on Saturday to prevent civil unrest
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.excerpt: France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday as the government seeks to prevent more civil unrest after some of the worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend. The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on ⁠Friday ⁠the security forces would include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues, adding that there had been social media calls for violence from “ultra-left” groups. “We are not talking about ⁠a peaceful, friendly demonstration,” Nuñez told reporters after a meeting of senior ministers and officials chaired by the president, Emmanuel Macron. “We are ready tomorrow to be ‌extremely firm and not tolerate anything.” Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais – where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display – are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend program. Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend’s hotspots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters. Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has caught it off guard six months before presidential elections to choose his successor.
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.trail: Security forces to include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism after worst street violence in years

/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.headline: Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.excerpt: Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend. Speaking after a meeting with intelligence officials and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed. Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but they might have to use alternative routes. The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.” Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the republic”. “The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.trail: French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations

/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.headline: Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.excerpt: Awa, 18, stood in the dock in the tribunal de Paris, a small, mute and bewildered figure seeming unable to understand, let alone answer, the simplest of questions. The court was told she had joined young people who looted an Yves Saint Laurent store on Boulevard Saint Germain in Paris’s Left Bank late on Sunday and stripped it bare within minutes. Awa was arrested at a nearby Métro station with a black balaclava and black gloves in her backpack along with four YSL handbags worth a total of €5,000 (£4,200). In the dock, dressed entirely in black – the clothes she was wearing when arrested two days earlier – she appeared panicked, clutched at her hair, picked her lip. Unable to speak, she covered her face and began to weep; first silently, then uncontrollably, her sobs punctuating an almost palpably painful silence. Awa was just one of 2,500 people arrested during last weekend’s rioting and looting across the country, more than 900 of whom are being fast-tracked through the courts using a procedure called comparution immédiate (immediate appearance). It sends them to trial straight or shortly after being taken into custody, or within three days if they are held in pretrial detention. The process of handling this sudden influx of cases has overwhelmed the courts and angered defendants’ lawyers, who say they have no time to meet clients. The violence erupted after high-school student and union demonstrations.
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.trail: Politicians have called for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty, and anger, behind their clients’ looting

/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.headline: ‘America, this is a warning’: pro- Trump Maga media in a froth over Europe protests
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.excerpt: Donald Trump sought to capitalize on the scenes of unrest in France, telling a crowd in Kansas on Monday that “migrants” and “communists” were responsible, and that the scenes were “what the radical ‘Dumocrats’ want to do to America”. As Republicans struggle to convince voters across the country ahead of November’s midterm elections, Trump’s allies in the conservative media have followed suit, seemingly hoping that the scenes in France can scare people to the polls. Sean Hannity, perhaps Fox News’ most prominent host, delivered his version of the message on Tuesday. Speaking over clips of fires in France, with the chyron “A warning from Europe” emblazoned on the screen, Hannity said: “This is, sadly I argue, by design – an attempt by the left to destroy the free world, western civilisation, if you will.” He added: “This is a preview of coming attractions here in America.” Hannity wasn’t alone. On Monday, Fox News host Laura Ingraham had on Jamie Metzl, who describes himself as a “technology and healthcare futurist [and] geopolitical expert”, to draw the same comparison. “If you like what you’re seeing in France then you should support these DSA candidates who are essentially calling for the same thing here,” Metzl said. He was only echoing something Ingraham herself had said a few days earlier, in front of a cartoon version of a police flashing light with the words “A warning to America”. The chyron, as she spoke, could not have had a clearer message.
/world/2026/oct/25/macrons-vandals-pay-b.trail: Fox News and others have toed president’s line – seemingly hoping unrest abroad will make people vote Republican

/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.headline: Kim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into China
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.excerpt: Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour. The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency. He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship. Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua. Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said. The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950. Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted. Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.trail: North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member

/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.headline: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.excerpt: For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side. Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia. The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby. It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border, named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow. “China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.trail: Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons

/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.headline: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.excerpt: Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping. Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary. In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record. Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation. The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.” China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment. A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said. The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.trail: Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say

/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.headline: China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.excerpt: Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending. China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%. China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures. Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%. Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful. “Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said. “Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.trail: Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand

/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.headline: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.excerpt: When Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods. “I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China. “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.” She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario. Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.” Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”. Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.
/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption.trail: The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies

/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.headline: Manhunt under way to find prisoner who absconded from medical facility
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.excerpt: A manhunt is under way to locate a prisoner who police say “poses a risk both to himself and the public” after he absconded from a medical facility in London. Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday, the Metropolitan police said. The force warned the public not to approach Lloyd, but instead to contact 999 if he is spotted. Lloyd was seen heading in the direction of Catford, police said in a statement on Saturday. Lloyd was convicted in 2025 of actual bodily harm, according to the Press Association, relating to an incident in Nottinghamshire involving three emergency services workers. He received a 12-month custodial sentence and was sent to prison. In September he was transferred to the medical facility in Lewisham. The 38-year-old is white and about 5ft 8in, of medium build with short dark hair. He was wearing a grey-blue T-shirt, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers when last seen at about 4.10pm on Friday, police said. Det supt Melanie Pressley, who is leading the manhunt, said: “We are conducting various significant inquiries to find Lloyd and return him to custody. “We are concerned he poses a risk both to himself and the public, and would urge anyone who sees him to call 999 immediately. Do not approach him.
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.trail: Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’

/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.headline: Met says it shared allegations about Meghan’s father with her but not other forces
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.excerpt: The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images. Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain. The police force said it had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s office, but it did not pass it on to “other law enforcement agencies”. The Sun newspaper published claims that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines. On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was “deeply distressed” by them. The duchess, who is estranged from her father said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them. Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US. Meghan’s father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”. The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.trail: Scotland Yard says it shared letter about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agencies

/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.headline: No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.excerpt: Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur. James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf. Other restaurants have opened in Dubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai. Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate. Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.” Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.trail: Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic

/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.headline: Is London really the most-taxed city? Banks accused of cherrypicking data
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.excerpt: A banking lobby group has been accused of cherrypicking data and trying to mislead the British government by claiming a tax rise for banks at next week’s budget would leave London less competitive than rival financial hubs. UK Finance, which represents banks including Lloyds, JP Morgan and Revolut, commissions an annual report tallying up all the taxes shouldered by a large bank, including corporation tax, social security, VAT and bank-specific levies. The report, put together by PwC, lists London as the most tax-intensive city, charging a “total tax rate” of 46.2%, compared with 42.2% in Amsterdam, 39.1% in Frankfurt, 29% in Dublin and 27.9% in New York. The figures have been heavily pushed by UK Finance, including in a recent letter to John Healey, the chancellor, in which it warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills. However, questions are now being raised about the lobby group’s data. They include why Paris, one of London’s biggest rival financial hubs and host to many large investment banks including JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and Barclays, has consistently been excluded from UK Finance comparisons. Calculations by the Guardian, which were reviewed by a leading accountancy firm, show that the same bank in Paris would face a total tax rate of between 51.6% and 57.3%. That is up to 11.1 percentage points higher than London.
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.trail: Lobby group’s figures, shared with John Healey, are misleading as they do not include major rival Paris, say campaigners

/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.headline: He wants to clean up the city and banish high prices. But who is ‘London’s Batman’?
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.excerpt: In the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets of London to tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering. “When I said I wanted to save London, I meant it. I will not stop until every single bit of trash is off the streets,” he says in a viral video, narrated in his trademark deep, husky and (suspiciously) American voice, joined by a gang of hooded helpers clearing rubbish-strewn streets in Tower Hamlets. This was Batman’s first good deed for the capital and, in the month since relocating from Gotham, he has carried out many more: paying parking fines for those visiting loved ones in hospital, giving out “free fuel” to motorists and bringing back £1 chicken and chips to those who once savoured this cheap and filling after-school meal. But who is he really and what does he stand for? In a recent interview with a BBC reporter, who was only given a time and location before the masked figure emerged in an alleyway, he summed up his mission: “People are struggling and I want to help them.” As for his identity, Niko Omilana – YouTuber, prankster and fifth-placed London 2021 mayoral candidate, who has pulled off similar stunts – is the most obvious guess, though he has denied it.
/uk-news/2026/oct/25/four-year-old-girl-.trail: The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-price Freddo bars

/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.headline: Carrick delivers 5min 27sec monologue and says he will hold brolly to keep everyone dry
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.excerpt: Michael Carrick began his Friday media conference with an extraordinary 5min 27sec monologue that cited Manchester United’s values of “humility”, “resilience” and “earning the right to win”, in what could be read as a public address to his players after the season’s dismal start. The head coach, whose job is under threat, later stated “100%” he could turn United’s form around and sought to underline his selfless attitude by saying he would hold an umbrella for “everyone else to stay dry” while he got wet. The downpour on Carrick intensified on Wednesday when Bruno Fernandes questioned his tactics after United’s 4-1 Champions League loss at Como and the coach did not rule out dropping the midfielder or stripping him of the captaincy when Bournemouth visit on Sunday. “I’ll always do what’s best for the football club,” he said. “The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost – the squad, the dynamics in the squad.” Carrick decided to make his speech, delivered without being asked a question, after events in Como and Lisandro Martínez’s criticism a week earlier of Jason Wilcox for the signings by the director of football. United have won only two of 11 games and started the current round of fixtures in 13th. Carrick said: “We need to respect what it takes to be here, respect what it takes to win, what you have to do to win. I’m not entitled to be here. Entitlement cannot be at this football club. We’re not entitled to win.
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.trail: Manchester United’s head coach said he would hold an umbrella for ‘everyone else to stay dry’ while he got wet as he underlined the importance of humility

/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.headline: Post-Ferguson worn-out horror show continues at Manchester United
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.excerpt: NIGHTMARE ON LAKE COMO We’re in the midst of what the kids call “spooky season” – or, for our fellow fusty old-timers out there, “autumn”. If you’ve been cosying up with a few horror flicks this month, you’ll know nothing good can come from hanging around a lake at this time of year. And so it proved for Manchester United, who endured an early Halloween nightmare on the banks of Lake Como that may have driven a stake through the Michael Carrick era. Hailed as the interim anti-Amorim not so long ago, Carrick has overseen two wins this season, against Ipswich and Sabah Baku. Como were in Serie D when Carrick won Big Cup with United as a player in 2008 – now, 18 years on, he watched the Italian upstarts dance, twirl and shimmy through the set of training cones he had sent out to represent his storied club. In the dugout, Carrick appeared frozen by fear. If there had been a sofa perched on the touchline, he may well have crouched behind it to avoid the series of jump-scares served up by his players. At the end, he walked over to the three United fans who had stuck around and held up his hands, looking like a cross between Ole Gunnar Solskjær and a doomed Squid Game contestant. But somehow, things were about to get worse. A week after Lisandro Martínez had taken aim at (or, in truth, just below) United’s hapless hierarchy, Bruno Fernandes decided to swing a little lower.
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.trail: In today’s Football Daily: A stake through the Michael Carrick era

/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.headline: ‘Angry’ Carrick on the brink as Fernandes hits out at Manchester United tactics
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.excerpt: Michael Carrick’s future as Manchester United manager is in the balance after a humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como on Wednesday night. Before Bournemouth’s visit to Old Trafford on Sunday his future may be discussed by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the co-owner who controls sporting policy. On a torrid night an “angry” Carrick insisted afterwards that he had not given his position any thought and was forced to defend himself against Bruno Fernandes after his captain questioned the manager’s tactics of not pressing against Cesc Fàbregas’s team. Carrick also criticised his side for not running. The defeat by Como in the third Champions League group game leaves United with only two wins all season from 11 games. Carrick’s side are in 13th place in the Premier League and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup last month. The 45-year-old was asked if he fears for his job. “Listen, I’ve not given my own position any thought,” he said. “[My thoughts are] for the supporters – I was one of them watching that and I wasn’t happy at all.” Carrick was then asked if he could walk away following the latest defeat in Europe. “No. It’s not about me right now and my feelings in that regard,” the manager said. “It’s more of as a team and as a football club, what we want to look like, what we should look like. And as I said, the results can come and go at times, but you got to do it in a certain way.
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.trail: The manager apologised to Manchester United fans after the 4-1 defeat in Como, while his captain criticised the team’s tactical approach

/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.headline: Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.excerpt: At the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot of the Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun. Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble. How do you solve what is, on revenue versus results, the worst-run club in world football? By changing the name of the latest patsy on the touchline, of course. For now a hard-fought point is perhaps enough to stave off that pre-programmed emergency response. Stand down the cowboy cops. Call off the blue and white saloons. Although with a run of Bournemouth, Chelsea, Aston Villa and Liverpool next up in the league it will no doubt soon be time to go out there and arrest Lee Harvey Oswald again. What’s that you say? OK, well, dig him up again. Re-arrest him. Whatever it takes. Someone has to stop these lone gunmen, these managerial magic bullet merchants from derailing the Manchester United supremacy.
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.trail: Getting rid of Michael Carrick is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different

/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.headline: ‘Like a fresh start’: Michael Carrick relieved by Manchester United’s draw at Leeds
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.excerpt: After a week in which Michael Carrick had “the headphones on” to quieten the noise, the Manchester United head coach claimed his side’s 1-1 draw at Leeds on Sunday “felt like a fresh start” and insisted that the season can still be a good one. Carrick’s team have seven points from seven Premier League games and have won only once in the competition, against Ipswich in August. Sunday’s draw followed the previous weekend’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham. Yet after a week in which United lost 2-0 at Atlético Madrid, after which Lisandro Martínez criticised the recruitment of the director of football, Jason Wilcox, Carrick was relieved at the point secured against Daniel Farke’s team. “[It’s been] quite quiet inside [the club] – the headphones have been on this week,” Carrick said. “It felt like a bit of a fresh start today – where we’re at and accepting it and doing something about it. That didn’t surprise me today. We’re not getting too carried away because we haven’t won the game, but if you keep doing the right things for the right reasons then you get what you deserve in the end. “It definitely shows that the boys are desperate to do well for each other as much as anything else and how much they appreciate playing for this club, because there was a real purpose to the group over the last couple of days and they took it on the pitch. There was an edge to the game, an intensity.
/football/2026/oct/25/manchester-united-.trail: Manchester United’s head coach Michael Carrick claimed the 1-1 draw at Leeds ‘felt like a fresh start’ and insisted the season can still be a good one
